essentials: The EUDR bans seven commodities and products made from them from the EU market unless they are **deforestation-free, legally produced and covered by a due diligence statement**.
The commodities are **cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood**. The cut-off date for deforestation is **31 December 2020**.
Proof goes down to the **plot of land**: the operator must provide geolocation data for where the commodity was produced.
After two postponements it applies from **30 December 2026** for large and medium companies and from **30 June 2027** for micro and small ones.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: Agricultural expansion drives most global deforestation, and EU consumption of a handful of commodities accounts for a significant share of it. The earlier EU Timber Regulation only covered wood and only legality. The EUDR, in force since June 2023, widens the list of commodities and adds a second test: a product can be perfectly legal in its country of origin and still be barred if the land was deforested after 2020.

sections.title: The three conditions
text: A relevant product may be placed on the EU market, made available on it or exported from it only if all three conditions are met.
steps: **Deforestation-free**: produced on land that was not converted from forest to agricultural use after 31 December 2020. For wood, harvesting must also not have caused forest degradation after that date.
**Legal**: produced in line with the relevant laws of the country of production, including land-use rights, environmental protection, labour rights and tax rules.
**Covered by a due diligence statement**: submitted to the EU information system before the product is placed on the market or exported.

sections.title: Who has to do what
text: The 2025 revision (Regulation (EU) 2025/2650) concentrated the burden on the company that first brings a product onto the EU market.

sections.title: The due diligence in three steps
steps: **Collect information**: product, quantity, country of production, supplier, and the **geolocation** of every plot where the commodity was produced. Plots of more than four hectares need a polygon; smaller ones a single point. For cattle, the locations where the animals were kept.

**Assess risk**: could the product be non-compliant? Criteria include the country's risk class, the presence of forests, the complexity of the supply chain and the risk of mixing with products of unknown origin.
**Mitigate risk**: where the risk is more than negligible, obtain more evidence, audits or satellite checks until it is negligible. Otherwise the product must not be placed on the market.
after: The Commission classifies countries as **low, standard or high risk**. Sourcing from low-risk countries allows simplified due diligence without the assessment and mitigation steps, and determines how many checks authorities carry out.

sections.title: Scope of products
text: Annex I lists the covered products by customs code. Besides the raw commodities it includes derived products such as chocolate, beef, palm oil derivatives, tyres, furniture, paper and plywood. A product not listed is out of scope even if it contains a listed commodity.

The list was adjusted in 2026 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102). Cattle hides and leather, retreaded tyres and several rubber articles were removed with effect from 18 September 2026. Some products were added, including soluble coffee and further palm oil derivatives; for these the rules apply from 30 December 2027.

sections.title: Enforcement
text: National competent authorities check operators and products, at a rate that depends on the risk class of the country of production, and customs verify that a valid statement reference accompanies each consignment. Penalties are set by Member States; the maximum fine must be at least 4% of the company's annual EU turnover. Authorities can also confiscate products and revenues and exclude companies from public procurement.

mistakes.right: Legality is only one of three conditions. Land deforested legally after 2020 still disqualifies the product.

mistakes.wrong: Only importers from tropical countries are affected.
mistakes.right: The regulation applies to products from every country, including EU Member States, and to exports.

mistakes.wrong: Every company in the chain files its own due diligence statement.
mistakes.right: Since the 2025 revision only the operator placing the product on the market for the first time does. Others keep traceability records.

mistakes.wrong: A certificate such as FSC or RSPO proves compliance.
mistakes.right: Certification can support the risk assessment but does not replace due diligence or the geolocation data.
Cattle hides and leather were removed from Annex I in September 2026.

practice: **Screen your product list against Annex I** by customs code, as amended in 2026.
**Determine your role** for each product flow: operator, downstream operator or trader.
As an operator, **collect geolocation data** from suppliers now. It is the part that takes longest.
**Register in the information system** and test how statements are filed, including through its interface for larger volumes.
**Define a risk assessment method** and what you do when risk is not negligible.
As a downstream company, **set up record-keeping** for reference numbers, suppliers and customers.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven EUDR commodities?
quiz.why: The seven are cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood. Cotton is not covered.

quiz.q: What is the cut-off date after which land must not have been deforested?
quiz.why: 31 December 2020. The other dates are the entry into force (June 2023) and the start of application (December 2026).

quiz.q: A shipment of soya was produced legally on land that was cleared of forest in 2022. Can it be placed on the EU market?
options: Yes, if the supplier is certified
quiz.why: All three conditions must be met. Legal deforestation after the cut-off date still bars the product.

quiz.q: Who must submit a due diligence statement after the 2025 revision?
options: The operator that first places the product on the EU market or exports it
Only the retailer selling to consumers
quiz.why: Downstream operators and traders no longer file their own statements; they keep traceability records.

quiz.q: What is required for a plot of land larger than four hectares?
options: A polygon describing the perimeter of the plot
A satellite image certified by a notary
Only the name of the region
quiz.why: Plots above four hectares need polygons; for smaller ones a single point is sufficient.

quiz.q: From when does the EUDR apply to large and medium-sized companies?
quiz.why: After two one-year postponements the date is 30 December 2026. Micro and small operators follow on 30 June 2027.

quiz.q: What does sourcing from a country classified as low risk allow?
options: Simplified due diligence without risk assessment and mitigation
Placing products on the market without geolocation data
quiz.why: Information must still be collected, including geolocation, but the assessment and mitigation steps are not required.

quiz.q: What is the minimum level of the maximum fine Member States must provide for?
options: 10% of the value of the goods
quiz.why: The regulation requires that the maximum fine be at least 4% of the operator's total annual turnover in the EU.
